deep.reconstruction:
Context (this folio together with 31v and 32v). Gauss is working on the biquadratic character of 1+i modulo a primary Gaussian modulus m=a+bi. On 32v he writes 'Det.(1+i) = 5/8(p-1) + 1/2(d-c)'. The method is a Gauss-lemma style count. Take a system of residues mod m and record, for each one, into which of four classes (labelled 0,1,2,3) it falls. The counts of these classes (a,b,c,d on the neighbouring pages) give the exponent of i. This page reduces those counts to sums of floor functions over lattice points.

(1) Top lines: the points (1/2)i and i are paired with (1/2)a+((1/2)b+1/2)i and (1/2)a+((1/2)b+1)i. These are shifts by m/2, i.e. the ends of lines parallel to m.

(2) Projection along m. A lattice point x+iy is moved parallel to m=a+bi onto the imaginary axis:
 x+iy - (x/a)(a+bi) = 0 + i(y - bx/a).
The line '1/2 . y - bx/a . 1' sets the strip condition 1/2 < y - bx/a < 1 (or with the endpoints taken as Gauss intends). This is the strip between the lines through i/2 and i parallel to m. Equivalently y lies between bx/a+1/2 and bx/a+1.

(3) After a shear by +x (passing to coordinates adapted to the parallelogram), the bounds become bx/a+1/2+x and bx/a+1+x. Only every second lattice point is wanted, because of the parity pattern of the class labels. So Gauss divides by 2:
 (bx/a+1/2+x)/2 = ((2b+2a)x+a)/(4a),
 (bx/a+1+x)/2 = ((2b+2a)x+2a)/(4a).
The '+2a' on the page belongs in the numerator.

(4) The quantities needed are therefore sums of floors such as Σ[(x+1)/2] and Σ[(x+1)/2] - Σ[x/2] for odd y ('für ungerade y'). These are counts of lattice points of a given parity class.

(5) Numerical table for a=13, b=16. Note that 13+16i is the example of 31v, with norm 425.
- Column 1 lists the multiples 58t of 2(a+b)=58, for t=0..8.
- Column 2 lists [58t/13] = 0,4,8,13,17,22,26,31,35.
- The marginal remainders +10, +3, +9 are 348, 406, 464 mod 13.
- Column 3 lists the values of column 2 mod 4: 0,0,0,1,1,2,2,3,3. It is continued as 3,0,0,1,1 for further t.

(6) The grid. Rows alternate '2 3 2 3 ...' and '1 0 1 0 ...'. This is the class label of x+iy depending only on the parities of x and y, i.e. on x+iy mod 2.
- Over the grid Gauss draws the square fundamental domain of a prime modulus. Its vertices are the circled 0, 2, 3 and an uncircled bottom vertex.
- Its sides go from the origin by 8 steps across and 5 up, and by 5 across and 8 down, i.e. the vectors 8+5i and its rotation 5-8i.
- The modulus is written below as 5+8i, with axes interchanged in the drawing; its norm is 89, a prime.
- The two diagonals are drawn, splitting the square into four triangles (the four 'quarter systems').
- The column 1,1,2,2,3 under '5+8i' and the rows '3 0 2 3 1 2 0 1 3' / '3 3 2 2 1 1 0' are per-row or per-column tallies of labels.

(7) Bottom right: the representatives 1-i, i, 1-i, i, ... are labelled 1 0 1 0 ... (a second row is struck out). The row 3, 3-i, 2, 2-i, 1, 1-i, 0 is labelled 3 3 2 2 1 1 0, i.e. by the real part rounded up. This illustrates how a label behaves along a line, matching the bracket sums Σ[(x+1)/2], Σ[x/2].

Overall: an Eisenstein-type lattice-point reformulation of a Gauss-lemma count for the quartic character of 1+i. It is tested numerically on 13+16i and 5+8i.
errors: '(2b+2a)x/(4a) + 2a' is a notational slip: the +2a belongs in the numerator, ((2b+2a)x+2a)/(4a) = (bx/a+1+x)/2.

The worked modulus 13+16i has norm 425 = 5^2*17, not a prime. Counts based on it test the floor-sum identities but not a character formula for prime moduli. Gauss may be deliberately testing the combinatorial identity only.
No arithmetic errors found in the table: [58t/13], the remainders 10, 3, 9 and the values mod 4 all check.

results.what: Reduction of the Gauss-lemma count for the quartic character of 1+i modulo a+bi to sums of floor functions [((2a+2b)x+a)/(4a)], [((2a+2b)x+2a)/(4a)]. The sums come from projecting lattice points along m onto the imaginary axis and counting by parity class.
results.modern_name: Lattice-point (Eisenstein-style) proof of the supplementary law of quartic reciprocity for 1+i via a Gauss lemma for Z[i]
results.usually_credited_to: Law stated by Gauss (TRB II, 1832) without proof. Published proofs came later (Lebesgue, Eisenstein, and others in the 1840s-50s); the lattice-point method for reciprocity is associated with Eisenstein (1844).

results.what: Square fundamental domain of residues mod 5+8i (norm 89), divided by its diagonals into four quarter-systems, with points labelled by class mod 2.
results.modern_name: Fundamental domain / quartic half-system in Gauss's lemma for Gaussian integers
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (quartic Gauss lemma idea, TRB II); Eisenstein

results.what: Table of [2(a+b)t/a] and its residues mod 4 for a=13, b=16

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss is known to have stated the 1+i supplementary law and to have had a Gauss-lemma approach in the Nachlass. A lattice-point/floor-sum reduction anticipating Eisenstein's geometric method is a notable unpublished detail, but not a new result.

checkable.asserts: Column 2 of the table equals [2(a+b)t/a] for a=13, b=16.
Column 3 is column 2 mod 4, including the continuation 3,0,0,1,1.
Second bound; the +2a belongs in the numerator.
Projection of x+iy along m=a+bi onto the imaginary axis.
5+8i has prime norm 89; 13+16i has composite norm 425.

transcription_corrections: First column: the top entry 0 overwrites an earlier figure, and 58 is overwritten. The '13' in the margin is the value a=13 (or a divisor note).
'für ungr. y' = 'für ungerade y' (for odd y).
Grid: the circled vertices are 0 (left), 2 (top) and 3 (right); the bottom vertex is uncircled. The square is spanned by 8+5i and 5-8i in drawing coordinates; the label '5+8i' gives the modulus.
In the last row '3 3-i 2 2-i 1 1-i 0' the leading 3 is a correction over another digit, and '2-i' is written over a struck character.
